props.title: Freedom
lines: The highest dividend money pays is control over your time.
Saving is not only for stuff. It is for options.

props.title: Richer, bigger homes — more worry

rows.v: 150,000 people in 140 countries: 45% of Americans felt 'a lot of worry' the previous day vs 39% globally.
55% of Americans felt 'a lot of stress' the previous day. Rest of world: 35%.
Median U.S. family income, inflation-adjusted: $29,000 in 1955, just over $62,000 in 2019.
Median American home: 983 square feet in 1950, 2,436 square feet in 2018. New homes: more bathrooms than occupants.

props.note: Book-dated Gallup and housing figures, 2020 text.

rows.v: A day-job path around $20,000 a year. He never took a taxi.
Living cost about $1,000 a month, earning about $1,800. The gap was the strategy.
He saved about $12,000 in two years, then quit to write.
Using money to buy control of your time is the most valuable use of money the book names.
Economist Robert Gordon: 46% agriculture, 35% crafts or manufacturing. Few jobs were 'think all day.'
38% of jobs are managers, officials, and professionals. Another 41% are service jobs that live in your head.
Factory work ended at the gate. Decision work does not. That is why extra income did not buy extra peace.
Bigger houses and faster cars, plus less control of time, can cancel. Happiness did not clearly rise with the $29k to $62k jump.
The highest-return purchase in the chapter is control of your waking hours.

props.title: Independence is the dividend
items: Save for options, not only for a sofa. Options are how you refuse a bad boss or a forced sale.
A modest life you control can beat a larger life that owns your calendar.
Housel's $12,000 at 22 was not a fortune. It was a permission slip to quit.
